<reason>Both sides built coherent comparative cases, but Side B won the decisive exchanges. B's core critique—that cameras only change the behavior of compliant, attentive drivers while fatalities cluster among non-responsive outliers (drunk, texting, unlicensed)—was sharpened in B4.5 and B5.3, and A never engaged the average-vs-outlier distinction, instead repeating the severity-universality logic that B had already reframed. A's repeated claim that CON "never showed" marginal yield from added stops became a mischaracterization after B4.1/B4.2 offered a plausible mechanism (targeted night/corridor enforcement) plus the seatbelt-campaign example, which directly answered A's pressure question. B also answered both pressure questions cleanly with the required A1/A2 structure and concrete reforms, while turning A's "solvable design choice" into the "pay or inform" problem voters repeal. A's strongest material—the certainty-vs-lottery frame, the externality asymmetry (fixable design choices vs. structural harms), and the point that stops impose the same fee spirals—was genuinely good and kept the externalities prong competitive, and A's designation-procedure answer was adequate. But A's rebuttals leaned on restating severity rather than resolving B's responsiveness objection, and the clipped opening plus the closing's inaccurate "never showed" claim were execution costs. B made the debate easier to decide and controlled the live clash on the "larger gains" prong while surviving the "fewer externalities" prong.
</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5–B4.6: "The people who fill the morgue are exactly the people least responsive to a fine arriving three weeks after the funeral. PRO's mechanism works best on the drivers least likely to die." This converted A's severity pivot into an unanswered distribution problem—lowering a corridor's average speed is not lowering the outlier's speed—and it framed the entire rest of the debate, including B's closing.
</best_rebuttal>
